strengths: First systematic study of training general-purpose code interpreters across 144 diverse reasoning tasks (not limited to math like prior work)
Clear problem diagnosis: rigorous mathematical analysis explaining why vanilla GRPO fails on heterogeneous tasks (Equations 4.3-4.5 showing vanishing signal when p(1-p)≈0)
Principled curriculum learning solution with theoretical justification: improvement potential Π_i = 4p_i(1-p_i) directly targets identified bottleneck
Solid empirical improvements: +9.3% RL gains from curriculum, consistent results across 3B/7B/14B model sizes
Comprehensive ablation studies validating importance of SFT warm-start, multi-turn framework, and improvement potential vs. difficulty
Practical engineering contribution: Code Execution Sandbox reduces training time by 39%
Emergent self-checking behavior discovered: ~15% of responses include code-based verification after training
Well-written with informative figures and detailed 26-page appendix including theoretical analysis
weaknesses: Marginal main improvement: R1-CI-14B achieves 72.4% vs. GPT-4o Code Interpreter's 70.9% (only 1.5% difference), questioning practical value given 1845 GPU hours required
Circular comparison with GPT-4o: uses GPT-4o-generated data for SFT training, then claims superiority over GPT-4o baseline
Severely limited generalization: only 37 held-out test tasks from same three benchmark sources as training data; no out-of-distribution evaluation on new domains or real-world coding
Reproducibility barriers: 1845 GPU hours required; code/model links missing; improvement potential estimation expensive (20 inferences per sample: 4 agents × 5 temperatures)

Theoretical assumptions don't fully hold: analysis assumes independent Bernoulli rewards but task samples are likely correlated; improvement potential estimated on SFT model but used during GRPO without guarantee of signal alignment
Missing key comparisons: no evaluation against recent reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek R1) or other code-reasoning systems beyond brief ToRL/ReTool mention
Hyperparameter choices unjustified: why 4 equal curriculum stages? Why these 4 agents? Why N=20 samples? Sensitivity analysis missing
Incomplete analysis of failures: many tasks remain at 0% accuracy even after training, with limited investigation into why
Evaluation concerns: uses GPT-4o for format normalization, no human evaluation, potential GPT-4o bias in correctness assessment
No analysis of which task properties benefit most from code vs. text, despite having capability taxonomy (Table 5)

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation on 144 diverse reasoning tasks covering multiple domains (math, spatial, logical, optimization, search)
Theoretically motivated multi-stage curriculum learning with clear mathematical analysis (Appendix C) showing why vanilla GRPO fails on heterogeneous data
Consistent empirical improvements across three model scales (3B/7B/14B) with solid ablation studies
Practical engineering contribution: Code Execution Sandbox reduces training time by 39% through CPU-GPU decoupling
Interesting observation of emergent self-checking behavior during training
Well-structured presentation with detailed task descriptions and capability classifications
weaknesses: Critical methodological flaw: model is trained on GPT-4o-generated trajectories for SFT, then claims to outperform GPT-4o—this comparison is fundamentally compromised and undermines the main claimed contribution
Limited novelty: combines existing techniques (SFT + GRPO from prior work + standard curriculum learning + straightforward potential metric) with incremental contribution
Weak baseline comparisons: missing evaluation against recent reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek-R1) and other RL+tool-use approaches; baselines are mostly variants of their own method

Insufficient validation of core hypothesis: no empirical demonstration that estimated improvement potential (p(1-p)) actually correlates with final performance gains; potential metric is estimated from only N=20 samples without sensitivity analysis

Theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis assumes binary Bernoulli rewards in controlled settings, but experiments involve heterogeneous multi-turn code generation; connection between theory and metric choice is post-hoc
Severe generalization limitations: evaluation restricted to symbolic reasoning with clear correctness criteria; no evidence of transfer to open-ended QA, generation tasks, or commonsense reasoning
Small test set (only 37 tasks) with no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars; many ablation improvements are modest
High reproducibility barriers: requires 16 H100 GPUs and 1845 hours training; dataset/model links appear blank; evaluation relies on GPT-4o for format normalization (circular dependency)
Limited investigation of self-checking behavior: observation is mostly descriptive; no ablation isolating its contribution to performance gains

strengths: First comprehensive study training code interpreters across 144 diverse reasoning and planning tasks, filling a significant gap beyond narrow domains like math
Theoretically well-motivated curriculum learning approach: clear analysis of why vanilla GRPO fails on heterogeneous data (Eq. 4.3-4.5) and principled improvement potential metric (Πᵢ = 4pᵢ(1-pᵢ))
Strong empirical results: R1-CI-14B achieves 72.4% on test tasks, outperforming GPT-4o Code Interpreter (70.9%) despite being 10x smaller and trained on GPT-4o generated data

Comprehensive evaluation: 144 standardized tasks from three benchmarks covering diverse reasoning skills (mathematical, spatial, logical, optimization, search); consistent improvements across 3B/7B/14B model sizes
Practical infrastructure contribution: Code Execution Sandbox decoupling execution from gradient computation reduces training time by 39% and enables larger batch sizes
Thorough experimental validation: comprehensive ablations on SFT necessity, curriculum effectiveness, base model choice, and multi-turn vs. single-turn approaches
Reproducibility: code, models, and datasets promised for release; training details well-documented
Interesting emergent behavior analysis: systematic study of self-checking behavior (Fig. 6a) suggests models autonomously discover useful verification strategies
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: multi-turn code/text is straightforward, GRPO from prior work, curriculum learning well-established; main novelty is improvement potential metric application, feeling somewhat incremental

Improvement potential metric lacks rigorous justification: why multiply by 4? Appears arbitrary beyond noting p=0.5 maximizes variance; uses only N=20 samples (4 agents × 5 temps) which is small and potentially noisy; missing ablations on N, agent diversity, and scaling factor; no correlation analysis with actual learning signal achieved

Curriculum design choices unjustified: why 4 equally-sized stages? Why 150 steps per stage? Sharp reward drops at transitions (Fig. 4b) suggest suboptimal design; no comparison with alternative curriculum strategies

Limited per-task analysis: no breakdown of results by task category (mathematical/spatial/logical); Figure 5 shows some tasks at 0% accuracy but doesn't identify which or why; unclear which task types benefit most from code interpreter training

Small test set with potential distribution shift: only 37 test tasks (25.7% of 144); all follow standardized formats so generalization unclear; close results (72.4% vs 70.9%) lack error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing

High computational cost and scalability concerns: requires 1845 GPU hours even with optimizations; expensive SFT data synthesis (requires running GPT-4o on all 107 tasks); only 107 tasks trained due to constraints; scalability to thousands of tasks unclear; approach likely inaccessible to most researchers

Response length finding (Figure 6c) underdeveloped: counterintuitive that multi-turn learning doesn't increase response length; three possible explanations provided with weak supporting evidence; actual response pattern analysis would strengthen

Some design choices unexplained: code execution caps (8 calls, 60s timeout) lack justification; hyperparameters (KL penalty 0.001, temperatures 1.0/0.6) and learning rate (1e-6) choice process unclear
Self-checking behavior analysis incomplete: observed but not rigorously analyzed; no ablation explicitly discouraging self-checking to quantify contribution to performance gains

Comparison limitations: GPT-4o Code Interpreter from 2024; comparison somewhat unfair as R1-CI specifically trained on 144 tasks vs. general-purpose model; missing comparisons with other recent code-augmented models

strengths: First comprehensive framework for training general-purpose Code Interpreter across 144 diverse reasoning tasks (vs. prior work limited to math domain)
Clear identification and theoretical analysis of why vanilla GRPO fails on mixed-difficulty tasks (policy signal vanishes at extremes)
Well-motivated improvement potential-guided curriculum learning (Πᵢ = 4pᵢ(1-pᵢ)) with solid theoretical grounding in gradient signal strength
Strong empirical results: R1-CI-14B achieves 72.4% accuracy, outperforming GPT-4o with Code Interpreter (70.9%), with RL gains improving from +3.4% to +9.3%
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations covering multiple RL algorithms, training strategies, and OOD generalization
Valuable 144-task benchmark curated from multiple sources with standardized format and detailed descriptions for reproducibility
Practical engineering contribution: Code Execution Sandbox reduces training time by 39% through decoupling GPU computation from CPU-based code execution
Discovery and documentation of emergent self-checking behavior learned without explicit training
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines existing techniques (multi-turn code generation, GRPO, curriculum learning) in relatively straightforward manner without significant methodological innovation

Theoretical analysis has gaps: connection between Πᵢ maximization at p=0.5 and optimality is loose; no comparison with alternative curriculum metrics (uncertainty, gradient norm, loss-based measures); analysis assumes Bernoulli rewards and ignores clipping/KL regularization

Generalization concerns: OOD performance gains are modest (AIME 24&25: 42% vs 30%); all 144 tasks from 3 specific benchmarks; unclear if approach generalizes to truly novel task types beyond this curated set

Improvement potential measurement overhead not fully characterized: computing Πᵢ requires 2,140+ inference calls; unclear if 39% training speedup includes this overhead; limits practical applicability for continual learning

Limited analysis of when and why code vs. text is chosen: no investigation of task-specific strategy learning; Figure 6b shows distribution but lacks interpretation; missing characterization of task properties benefiting from curriculum

Evaluation limitations: binary success/failure metric only (no partial credit or reasoning quality); rule-based evaluation may miss correct answers in non-standard formats; large performance gaps across task categories (BBH 86.5% vs ~60-70% others) unexplained

High computational cost remains substantial: 1845 GPU hours for 14B model even with optimization; multi-turn inference slower than baselines; practical applicability limited for resource-constrained settings; no cost comparison with baselines

Experimental design: GPT-4o used only for SFT data generation, not direct competitor with identical setup; comparison with GPT-4o API may not be fair; no comparison with recent reasoning models (o1, Claude 3.5); missing ablation of whether stronger SFT helps baseline methods
Curriculum design choices not justified: why 4 stages with these specific IP ranges? Why 150 steps per stage? Why 4 agent variants? Figure 10 suggests single RL round sufficient—implications unclear
Paper length (29 pages) with key details in appendix; improvement potential metric derivation could be more intuitive; some presentation could be more concise

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly demonstrates real limitation where vanilla GRPO fails on heterogeneous tasks (gains drop from 27.4% with 1 task to 3.3% with 107 tasks)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 144 diverse tasks across multiple sources with standardized format, three model sizes, and consistent improvements across all scales
Clear mathematical grounding: Section 4.2-4.3 provides transparent analysis connecting Bernoulli variance p(1-p) to learning signal strength
Strong empirical results: outperforms GPT-4o text-only (58.6%) and GPT-4o with Code Interpreter (70.9%) on diverse reasoning tasks
Practical engineering contribution: Code Execution Sandbox achieves 39% speedup through CPU/GPU decoupling
Extensive ablation studies: evaluates SFT design choices, RL algorithms, warm vs. cold start, and online vs. offline training
Reproducibility commitment: detailed hyperparameters, task descriptions, and promise to release code and models
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution reduces to applying straightforward curriculum learning (ordering samples by improvement potential Π_i = 4p_i(1-p_i)) to Code Interpreter training
Shallow theoretical analysis: Bernoulli variance property (Eq 4.4) and Lemma D.2 restate well-known results; Remark D.1 acknowledges analysis ignores clipping without addressing it
Fairness concerns in comparison: uses GPT-4o-generated training data (6.5k trajectories), then claims to outperform GPT-4o, raising circularity questions about benchmark validity
Hidden computational cost: improvement potential measurement requires 20 forward passes per sample (4 agents × 5 temperatures) but this cost is not included in reported 1845 GPU hours
Arbitrary design choices: why 4 stages (not 3 or 8)? Why equal group boundaries? Why factor of 4 in Π_i formula? Ablations for these critical choices are missing
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; claims lack statistical significance
Performance degradation in Stage 4: Figure 4 shows score plateauing or declining when adding low-potential samples, suggesting fundamental limitation inadequately discussed
Poor performance on many tasks: Figure 5 shows numerous tasks with very low scores; absolute performance on AIME remains low (15% for 7B)
Missing alternative comparisons: no comparison to prioritized experience replay, other curriculum learning methods, importance weighting schemes, or different potential ranking functions
Uncertain generalization: all 144 tasks involve code execution; unclear if curriculum-by-potential applies to other reasoning domains or only code-centric tasks
Attribution gap: SFT alone contributes ~16% improvement (44.1%→60.1%), while GRPO curriculum learning adds only ~12% (60.1%→72.4%), weakening novelty claims
Incomplete cost-benefit analysis: does expensive potential measurement justify modest RL gains (3.4%→9.3%)?

strengths: First comprehensive study training general-purpose Code Interpreter across 144 diverse reasoning/planning tasks spanning multiple domains
Strong empirical results: R1-CI-14B achieves 72.4% accuracy, outperforming GPT-4o with Code Interpreter (70.9%) and text-only (58.6%)
Well-motivated theoretical analysis: sound mathematical justification for why vanilla GRPO fails on mixed-difficulty batches using Bernoulli variance analysis
Extensive experimental validation with thorough ablation studies (multi-turn vs. single-turn, SFT design, warm vs. cold start, RL algorithms, offline vs. online training)
Practical engineering contribution: Code Execution Sandbox reduces training time by 39% (4500→1845 GPU hours) through GPU-CPU decoupling
Analysis of emergent behaviors: documents self-checking through code generation and code usage patterns
Clear presentation with good use of figures; implementation details and 144 task descriptions provided for reproducibility
Consistent improvements across multiple model sizes (3B, 7B, 14B) and OOD evaluation on GPQA and AIME benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited novelty in core components: SFT+GRPO is standard (DeepSeek R1), multi-stage curriculum learning is well-established, and improvement potential metric Πᵢ=4pᵢ(1-pᵢ) is essentially Bernoulli variance. Main contribution is their combination, which is incremental

Fairness concerns in comparisons: (1) Using GPT-4o to generate SFT training data then comparing against GPT-4o is somewhat circular; (2) Missing comparisons with other recent reasoning models; (3) No explicit statement that GPT-4o was evaluated with identical sandbox settings/timeouts
Improvement potential estimation robustness: Only 20 samples (5 temperatures × 4 agents) to estimate Πᵢ; no sensitivity analysis provided; stability of ranking across different seeds not discussed

Statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests on main results; unclear if single or multiple runs; test set size is only 37 tasks from 144 total; no per-task error analysis

Incomplete analysis of key contributions: (1) Emergent self-checking only demonstrated qualitatively; (2) No failure case analysis or systematic error characterization; (3) Missing analysis of when code execution is beneficial vs. harmful; (4) No quantitative breakdown of self-checking utility
Limited generalization analysis: All tasks are reasoning/planning focused; OOD evaluation limited to 2 benchmarks; unclear how approach transfers to other domains

Methodological questions: (1) Why multiply by 4 in Eq. 4.6? Scaling factor lacks justification; (2) Hyperparameter selection (4 stages, 150 steps per stage) not explained; (3) SFT data sensitivity not analyzed; (4) Simple rule-based rewards—learned rewards not explored
Second-round training failure (Figure 10) unexplained; Figure 3d dramatic drop lacks deep analysis of whether due to heterogeneity alone or compounded by sparse rewards
Large computational cost (1845 GPU hours) still limits independent reproducibility; inference time and cost comparison with GPT-4o not provided
